intro:
**The Break of Dawn and the Serene Soul**

Al-Fajr, "The Dawn," is the eighty-ninth chapter of the Qur'an, comprising 30 verses of early Makkan revelation. It opens with five solemn, mysterious chronological oaths: *“By the dawn, and by ten nights, and by the even and the odd, and by the night when it passes—is there in that an oath for one possessed of intellect?”* (89:1–5). The "ten nights" are universally interpreted in classical hadith literature (including Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 969) as the sacred first ten days of Dhū al-Ḥijjah—the pinnacle of the spiritual and pilgrimage year. Sūrah al-Fajr is celebrated for its sweeping historical warnings about the ruined civilizations of ancient Arabia (Iram of the Pillars, Thamūd, and Pharaoh), its searing socio-economic critique of orphan neglect and greed, and its peerless, immortal conclusion in verses 27–30, which welcomes the tranquil, purified spirit into the Divine Presence: *“O tranquil soul (*Yā ayyatuhā al-nafsu al-muṭma'innah*)! Return to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing [to Him]!”*

**The Structural Architecture and the Four Movements**

The architecture of Sūrah al-Fajr unfolds across four dramatic movements:
1. The Oaths of Time and the Ruins of Tyranny (1–14): Swears by the dawn, the ten nights, the even and odd, and the passing night, reviewing the sudden destructions of ʿĀd, Thamūd, and Pharaoh to show that God is ever watchful over human tyranny.
2. The False Calculus of Wealth and the Neglect of Orphans (15–20): Delivers a profound psychological diagnosis of human arrogance: when God tests man with honor and wealth, he boasts: *“My Lord has honored me!”*, but when He tests him with restricted provision, he complains: *“My Lord has humiliated me!”* (89:15–16). It strikes at the heart of their societal cruelty: *“No! But you do not honor the orphan, and you do not encourage one another to feed the impoverished, and you consume inheritance devouringly, and you love wealth with immense love!”* (89:17–20).
3. The Shattering of the Earth and the Regret of Life (21–26): The apocalyptic climax: when the earth is leveled, pounded powder upon powder (*dakkan dakkā*), and your Lord comes with the angels rank upon rank, and Hell is brought near on that Day! He will cry the tragic, immortal regret of verse 24: *“Oh, I wish I had put forward [good deeds] for my true life (*Yā laytanī qaddamtu li-ḥayātī*)!”*
4. The Serene Soul: Al-Nafs al-Muṭma'innah (27–30): The sūrah concludes with the gentlest, most exquisite invitation in all of sacred scripture: *“O tranquil soul (*Yā ayyatuhā al-nafsu al-muṭma'innah*)! Return to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing [to Him]! And enter among My [righteous] servants! And enter My Paradise!”*

All transgressed through corruption and tyranny, yet *“your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment; indeed, your Lord is ever watchful (*inna Rabbaka la-bi-l-mirṣād*)!”* (89:13–14).

verses.1:
> By the dawn

**The Sūrah Opens on the Dawn**

The sūrah opens on the oath, and the first of the oaths is the oath of the dawn. The sūrah takes its name from this first word, and the name is the name of the dawn. The dawn is the moment of the opening of the day, and the opening of the day is the opening that the sūrah's first verse states. The sūrah's structure is the structure of the oath: the oaths run from this verse to the fifth, where the oaths are gathered into the question of the sufficient oath. The sūrah's first movement is the movement of the oaths, and the four oaths are the dawn, the ten nights, the even and the odd, and the night when it passes. The sūrah's first verse is the door of the first movement, and the door opens on the dawn.

**The Dawn as the First Oath**

The dawn is the first of the four oaths, and the dawn is the moment that the Book names in its standing verses. The dawn is the moment of the light that breaks the darkness of the night, and the breaking is the breaking that the sūrah's oath assumes. The sūrah's use of the dawn as the oath is the sūrah's way of placing the sūrah's warning under the witness of the day, and the day is the day that opens on the dawn. The Book swears by the dawn in its standing form, and the standing form is the form of the statement that the dawn is the dawn of the opening of the day. The sūrah's first oath is thus the oath that the sūrah places at the beginning of the sūrah's argument, and the argument is the argument of the oaths and their warning.
verses.2:
> and the ten nights

**The Three Readings of the Ten Nights**

The tradition records the ten nights in three readings, and the three readings are the three moments of the Islamic year. The first reading takes the ten nights to be the break of dawn at the beginning of the first month of the Islamic calendar, and the first month is the month of the beginning. The second reading takes the ten nights to be the break of dawn at the feast of the sacrifice at the end of the pilgrimage, and the feast is the feast of the sacred month of the pilgrimage. The Book states the sacred days in its standing verse: "Complete the pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage for Allah" (2:196).

**The Ten Nights of the Fasting**

The third reading, the reading of the ten nights of the month of the fasting, is the reading that the sūrah's context favors, and the context is the context of the revelation of the Book. The ten nights are the last ten nights of the month, and the last ten nights are the nights of the Night of the Decree. The report of the Messenger of God ﷺ states the seeking of the Night of the Decree in the form of the command, and the command is the command to seek it in the odd nights of the last ten nights, and the report is the report recorded in the standing form of the Ṣaīḥ. The sūrah's ten nights, on this reading, are the ten nights of the seeking, and the seeking is the seeking of the Night of the Decree in the odd of the ten. The reading is thus the reading that the sūrah's oath carries in its fullest form, and the fullest form is the form of the last ten nights of the month of the fasting.
verses.3:
> and the even and the odd

**The Third Oath**

The third oath of the sūrah is stated in this verse, and the third oath is the oath of the even and the odd. The previous verse stated the ten nights, and the sūrah now states the division of the ten into the even and the odd, and the division is the division that the sūrah's third oath names. The sūrah's order is the order of the oaths in their relation: the ten nights are the whole, and the even and the odd are the two of the whole. The even and the odd are the third of the four oaths, and the four are the dawn and the ten nights and the even and the odd and the night when it passes. The sūrah's first movement is now at its third verse, and the movement is the movement of the five verses.

**The Many Readings**

The tradition records the verse in the form of the many, and the many is the many that the tradition states in its number. The commentators have given the verse up to thirty-six different interpretations, and the thirty-six are the thirty-six that the tradition records. The sūrah's verse carries the thirty-six, and the thirty-six are the sūrah's way of stating the breadth of the oath. The breadth is the breadth of the even and the odd in the created order, and the created order is the created order that the sūrah's oath names. The sūrah's third oath is thus the oath of the breadth, and the breadth is the breadth that the tradition records in its thirty-six.

**The Even and the Odd in the Creation**

The first reading of the verse takes the even to be all of the creation and the odd to be the One who is without peer. The Book states the creation in pairs in its standing verse: "and created you in pairs" (78:8). The standing verse states the even of the creation, and the sūrah's verse states the odd of the One, and the two together are the two of the created order. The even is the even of the pairs, and the odd is the odd of the One who is One without peer, and the two are the two of the sūrah's oath in the form of the creation. The reading is the reading of the creation, and the creation is the creation that the sūrah's oath names.
verses.4:
> and the night when it passes

**The Night in Its General**

The first reading of the verse takes the night to be the night in general, and the night in general is the night that the sūrah's oath names in its full form. The reading states the night in the form of the Wisdom, and the Wisdom is the Wisdom of the measuring between the night and the day. The sūrah's verse, on this reading, is the oath of the measuring, and the measuring is the measuring of the Lord between the two: the night and the day. The reading is the reading recorded in the standing form of the tafsīr, and the reading is the reading that places the oath in the form of the Wisdom.

**The Passing of the Night**

The form of the verse is the form of the passing, and the passing is the passing of the night in its motion. The sūrah's naming is the naming of the night in its motion: the night is not the night that is still; the night is the night that passes. The sūrah's fourth oath is thus the oath of the motion, and the motion is the motion of the night in its passing. The sūrah's first movement is the movement of the oaths in their forms, and the forms are the forms of the dawn and the nights and the even and the odd and the passing.
verses.5:
> Is all this ˹not˺ a sufficient oath for those who have sense

**The Question of the Sufficient Oath**

The fifth verse of the sūrah gathers the four oaths into the question, and the question is the question of the sufficient oath. The four oaths were the oath of the dawn, the oath of the ten nights, the oath of the even and the odd, and the oath of the night when it passes, and the sūrah now asks whether the four are the sufficient oath for the one who has sense. The sūrah's method is the method of the question: the oaths are stated, and the oaths are asked whether they suffice, and the asking is the asking that states the weight of the warning that follows. The sūrah's first movement is complete in this verse, and the completion is the completion of the five verses.

**The Sufficiency of the Oaths**

The question of the sūrah is the question of the sufficiency, and the sufficiency is the sufficiency of the four oaths for the one who has sense. The sūrah does not ask whether the oaths are true; the sūrah asks whether the oaths suffice, and the sufficing is the sufficing of the witness for the one who reflects. The sūrah's method is the method of the Book at its moments of the oath: the oaths are the witnesses, and the witnesses are sufficient for the one who has sense, and the one who has sense is the one whose intellect prevents him from the refusal of the witness. The sūrah's question is thus the question that states the weight of the oaths, and the weight is the weight that suffices for the one who reflects.
verses.6:
> Did you not see how your Lord dealt with ’Ȃd—

**The Second Movement Opens**

The sūrah's second movement opens in this verse, and the second movement is the movement of the three peoples. The previous verse gathered the four oaths into the question of the sufficient oath, and the sūrah now states the first of the three peoples, and the first people is 'Ād. The sūrah's order is the order of the three peoples: 'Ād first, then Thamûd, and then Pharaoh. The three peoples are the three witnesses of the sūrah's warning, and the three are the three that the sūrah's first movement guaranteed in its oaths. The sūrah's second movement is now at its first verse, and the movement is the movement of the eight verses.

**The People of the South**

The people of 'Ād are the pre-Islamic tribe of the south of the Arabia, and the tribe is the tribe that rejected the prophet who was sent to it. The Book states the account of 'Ād in its standing verses, and the standing form is the form of the statement that 'Ād is the people of the prophet. "And to the people of ’Âd We sent their brother Hûd" (11:50). Worship Allah—you have no god but Him'" (7:65). "As for ’Ȃd, they acted arrogantly throughout the land with no right" (41:15). "’Ȃd ˹also˺ rejected ˹the truth˺. Then how ˹dreadful˺ were My punishment and warnings!" (54:18). The four standing verses state the four of the account of 'Ād: the sending of the prophet, the calling of the prophet, the arrogance of the people, and the rejection of the people.

**The Form of the Question**

The form of the verse is the form of the question, and the question is the question of the seeing. The sūrah does not state the dealing of the Lord with 'Ād; the sūrah asks whether the one addressed has seen the dealing, and the seeing is the seeing of the event rather than the seeing of the place. The sūrah's question is the question of the Book at its moments of the warning: the warning is placed under the witness of the seen, and the seen is the seen that the sūrah's question assumes. The sūrah's verse is thus the verse of the seeing, and the seeing is the seeing of the dealing of the Lord with 'Ād.

**The Dealing of the Lord**

The dealing of the Lord with 'Ād is the dealing that the sūrah's second movement will state in its verses, and the dealing is the dealing of the punishment. The sūrah's question asks the one addressed to see the dealing, and the dealing is the dealing that the sūrah's thirteenth verse will complete in the form of the scourge. The sūrah's method is the method of the question and the answer: the question is stated in this verse, and the answer is stated in the verses that follow it. The sūrah's second movement is thus the movement of the question and the answer, and the question is the question of the dealing, and the answer is the answer of the transgression and the punishment.
verses.7:
> ˹the people˺ of Iram—with ˹their˺ great stature

**The Legend of the City**

The tradition records the legend of the city in the form of the building, and the building is the building that the legend states. Several sources cite the Arabian legend that the city was built by the son of 'Ād, and the son is the son of the legend in the form of the king. The legend is the legend of the Arabian folklore, and the folklore is the folklore that states the city in its pillars and its gold and its silver. The Book of the tafsīr records the legend in the form of the paradise, and the paradise is the paradise that the legend states as the lofty structure standing on the tall pillars, built with the gold and the silver and studded with the jewels and the gems. The legend is the legend that the sūrah's epithet assumes, and the assuming is the assuming that the sūrah's verse carries in its form of the city.
verses.8:
> unmatched in any other land

**The Unmatched Stated**

The epithet of 'Ād is completed in this verse, and the completion is the completion in the form of the unmatched. The previous verse stated the name of 'Ād in its Iram and its pillar, and the sūrah now states the epithet in its unmatched, and the unmatched is the unmatched in any other land. The sūrah's two verses of 'Ād are the name and the epithet, and the two together are the 'Ād in its complete form. The sūrah's second movement is now at its third verse, and the movement is the movement of the eight verses.

**The Land of the Unmatched**

The unmatched of the verse is the unmatched in any other land, and the land is the land of the created order. The sūrah's statement is the statement of the relation of the unmatched to the land: 'Ād was unmatched in its land, and the land was the land of the south of the Arabia. The sūrah's naming of the land is the naming of the land in its contrast: the unmatched of 'Ād in its land, and the matching of the lands in their other. The sūrah's verse is the sūrah's way of stating the unmatched in its land, and the land is the land that the sūrah's epithet names. The unmatched is thus the unmatched of the one land over the other lands, and the one land is the land of 'Ād.

**The Arrogance of the Unmatched**

The unmatched of 'Ād is the unmatched that the Book states in the form of the arrogance, and the arrogance is the arrogance of the boasting. The Book states the arrogance of 'Ād in its standing verse: "As for ’Ȃd, they acted arrogantly throughout the land with no right, boasting, 'Who is superior to us in beauty?'" (41:15). The standing verse states the two together: the arrogance throughout the land, and the boasting of the superiority. The sūrah's unmatched is the unmatched of the standing verse, and the standing verse is the form of the Book's law of the unmatched.
verses.9:
> and Thamûd who carved ˹their homes into˺ the rocks in the ˹Stone˺ Valley

**The People of the North**

The people of Thamûd are the pre-Islamic tribe of the north of the Arabia, and the tribe is the tribe that rejected the prophet who was sent to it. The Book states the account of Thamûd in its standing verses, and the standing form is the form of the statement that Thamûd is the people of the prophet. "And to the people of Thamûd We sent their brother Ṣâliḥ. He said, 'O my people! Worship Allah—you have no god but Him'" (7:73). "The people of Thamûd rejected the messengers" (26:141). "Thamûd rejected the warnings ˹as well˺" (54:23). The four standing verses state the four of the account of Thamûd: the sending of the prophet, the calling of the prophet, the rejection of the messengers, and the rejection of the warnings. The sūrah's Thamûd is the Thamûd of the standing verses, and the standing verses are the form of the Book's law of Thamûd.

**The Carving of the Rocks**

The mark of Thamûd is the mark of the carving, and the carving is the carving of the rocks in the valley. The sūrah's naming is the naming of the people by their work: Thamûd is the people who hollowed the rocks, and the hollowing is the hollowing that states the work of the people in the stone. The valley is the valley of the stone, and the stone is the stone of the valley of the people.

**The Second of the Three Peoples**

The three peoples are the three of the sūrah's argument, and the argument is the argument of the transgression and the punishment. The sūrah's second people is the people of the rock, and the next people will be the people of the structure, and the two together with the first are the three of the sūrah's second movement. The sūrah's verse is the verse of the second people, and the second people is the people of the valley of the stone.

"And to the people of Thamûd We sent their brother Ṣâliḥ" (11:61).
verses.10:
> and the Pharaoh of mighty structures

**The Third People Named**

The third people of the sūrah's second movement is named in this verse, and the third people is Pharaoh. The previous verses stated the first people, 'Ād, in its three verses, and the second people, Thamûd, in its one verse, and the sūrah now states the third people in its one verse, and the one verse is the verse of the structure. The sūrah's order is the order of the three peoples: 'Ād first, then Thamûd, and then Pharaoh. The three peoples are now stated in their five verses, and the five verses are the five of the first half of the second movement. The sūrah's second movement is now at its fifth verse, and the movement is the movement of the eight verses.

**The Word of the Structure**

The word the sūrah gives Pharaoh is the word of the mighty structure, and the structure is the mark of the people in its building. The tradition records the word in the form of the tent peg, and the tent peg is the peg of the tent of the dwelling. The Book states the same word for Pharaoh in its standing verse: "Before them, the people of Noah denied ˹the truth˺, as did ’Âd, Pharaoh of the mighty structures" (38:12). The standing verse states the word in the same form, and the form is the form of the Book's law of the word. The sūrah's Pharaoh is the Pharaoh of the standing verse, and the standing verse is the form that the sūrah's verse assumes. The sūrah's third people is thus the people of the structure, and the structure is the structure that the standing verse names.

**The Three Marks of the Three Peoples**

The three peoples of the sūrah are the three marks of the sūrah's second movement, and the three marks are the pillar and the carving and the structure. The first people is marked by the pillar of the stature, the second people is marked by the carving of the rock, and the third people is marked by the structure of the building. The three marks are the three of the sūrah's argument, and the argument is the argument of the greatness of the created that the sūrah's warning meets. The sūrah's contrast of the three marks is the sūrah's way of stating the breadth of the greatness: the greatness of the body in 'Ād, the greatness of the work in Thamûd, and the greatness of the building in Pharaoh. The three together are the three of the sūrah's second movement.
verses.11:
> They all transgressed throughout the land

**The Transgression Stated**

The sūrah's statement of the three peoples moves now from the naming to the transgression, and the transgression is stated in this verse. The five previous verses of the second movement named the three peoples in their marks, and the sūrah now states the transgression that the three shared, and the transgression is the transgression throughout the land. The sūrah's order is the order of the naming and the transgression: the naming in the five verses, and the transgression in the two verses that follow. The sūrah's second movement is now at its sixth verse, and the movement is the movement of the eight verses.

**The Three Together**

The tradition states the verse in the form of the three, and the three are the three peoples together. The verse refers to all three groups mentioned in the verses of the naming, and the three are 'Ād and Thamûd and Pharaoh. The sūrah's statement is the statement of the relation of the transgression to the three: the transgression is the transgression that the three shared, and the sharing is the sharing that the sūrah's verse states. The sūrah's method is the method of the gathering: the three are gathered in the one transgression, and the one transgression is the transgression that the three shared. The sūrah's verse is the sūrah's way of gathering the three in their transgression, and the gathering is the gathering of the three witnesses of the sūrah's warning.
verses.12:
> spreading much corruption there

**The Corruption Stated**

The second verse of the transgression is stated in this verse, and the second verse is the verse of the corruption. The previous verse stated the transgression of the three peoples in their land, and the sūrah now states the corruption that followed the transgression, and the corruption is the corruption that was spread in the land. The sūrah's order is the order of the two: the transgression first, and the corruption after. The corruption is the corruption that completes the sūrah's statement of the transgression, and the completion is the completion of the two verses. The sūrah's second movement is now at its seventh verse, and the movement is the movement of the eight verses.

**The Corruption of the Three**

The corruption of the verse is the corruption of the three peoples together, and the three are the three that the sūrah's eleventh verse gathered in their transgression. The sūrah's statement is the statement of the relation of the corruption to the three: the corruption is the corruption that the three shared, and the sharing is the sharing that the sūrah's verse states. The three peoples corrupted the land in their several ways, and the several ways are the several of the three marks: the pillar of the stature, the carving of the rock, and the structure of the building. The sūrah's verse is the sūrah's way of stating the corruption of the three, and the corruption is the corruption that the three shared in their land.
verses.13:
> So your Lord unleashed on them a scourge of punishment

**The Punishment Stated**

The sūrah's second movement reaches its punishment in this verse, and the punishment is the punishment of the scourge. The seven previous verses of the movement stated the three peoples in their naming and their transgression, and the sūrah now states the punishment that the transgression received, and the punishment is the punishment that the Lord unleashed on the three. The sūrah's order is the order of the cause and the effect: the cause in the seven verses, and the effect in this verse. The sūrah's second movement is now at its eighth verse, and the movement is the movement of the eight verses.

**The Word of the Scourge**

The word the sūrah gives the punishment is the word of the scourge, and the scourge is the whip that is woven of the various materials. The tradition records the word in the form of the mixed, and the mixed is the mixed of the punishment in its two meanings. The first meaning is the nature of the punishment, and the nature is the nature in which the blood and the flesh are said to be mixed together. The second meaning is the various punishments that afflicted the three peoples, and the various are the various that the tradition records in its three.

**The Three Punishments**

The three punishments of the three peoples are the three that the tradition records in the form of the scourge. The first punishment is the howling, raging wind that was sent on the tribe of 'Ād, and the Book states it in its standing verse: "And as for ’Ȃd, they were destroyed by a furious, bitter wind" (69:6). "Indeed, We sent against them a furious wind, on a day of unrelenting misery" (54:19). The second punishment is the overwhelming earthquake that struck the tribe of Thamûd, and the Book states it in its standing verse: "As for Thamûd, they were destroyed by an overwhelming blast" (69:5). "Then an ˹overwhelming˺ earthquake struck them, and they fell lifeless in their homes" (7:78). The third punishment is the drowning of Pharaoh and his host, and the Book states it in its standing verse: "And ˹remember˺ when We parted the sea, rescued you, and drowned Pharaoh’s people before your very eyes" (2:50). The three standing verses state the three punishments, and the three are the three of the sūrah's scourge in its various.

**The Continuity of the Punishment**

The tradition states the verse in the form of the continuity, and the continuity is the continuity of the punishment in its two worlds. The pouring of the scourge indicates the continuous nature of the punishment, and the punishment is the punishment that is realized in this life and the next. The sūrah's statement is the statement of the relation of the punishment to the two worlds: the punishment of this world is the punishment of the wind and the earthquake and the drowning, and the punishment of the next is the punishment that the sūrah's fifth movement will state in its Fire.
verses.14:
> ˹For˺ your Lord is truly vigilant

**The Second Movement Closes**

The sūrah's second movement is closed in this verse, and the closing is the closing in the form of the vigilance. The previous verse stated the punishment of the three peoples in its scourge, and the sūrah now states the ground of the punishment, and the ground is the vigilance of the Lord. The sūrah's order is the order of the punishment and the ground: the punishment in the eighth verse, and the ground in this verse. The sūrah's second movement is complete in this verse, and the completion is the completion of the eight verses.

**The Word of the Vigilance**

The word the sūrah gives the Lord is the word of the vigilant, and the vigilant is the one who lies in ambush. The translation of the verse is the translation of the vigilant, and the vigilant is the vigilant that the sūrah's verse states. The tradition records the word in the form of the watchfulness, and the watchfulness is the watchfulness that nothing escapes from. The sūrah's verse is the sūrah's way of stating the Lord in its vigilance, and the vigilance is the vigilance that the sūrah's second movement closes on.

**Nothing Escapes**

The tradition states the verse in the form of the nothing-escaping, and the nothing-escaping is the nothing-escaping of the watchfulness. Nothing escapes the Lord, and the Lord hears what the people say in public and in private, and the Lord sees what they do in public and in private, and the Lord rewards or punishes them accordingly. The statement is the statement recorded in the standing form of the tafsīr, and the statement is the statement of the vigilance in its full form.

**The Respite of the Tyrants**

The point of the verse is the point of the respite, and the respite is the respite that the Lord allows for the tyrants. No matter what respite the Lord may allow for the tyrants to work their corruption, they will be punished for it in due time. The Book states the respite in its standing verses: "Those who disbelieve should not think that living longer is good for them. They are only given more time to increase in sin" (3:178). "Many are the societies whose end We delayed while they did wrong, then seized them. And to Me is the final return" (22:48). The two standing verses state the two of the respite: the respite that is the increase in the sin, and the respite that is the seizing in the due time. The sūrah's vigilance is the vigilance of the standing verses, and the standing verses are the form of the Book's law of the respite.

**The Ground of the Punishment**

The sūrah's statement is the statement of the relation of the ground to the punishment: the vigilance is the ground, and the punishment is the effect that the ground produces. The sūrah's second movement is the movement of the ground and the effect: the ground is the vigilance of the Lord, and the effect is the scourge of the three peoples.
verses.15:
> Now, whenever a human being is tested by their Lord through ˹His˺ generosity and blessings, they boast, “My Lord has ˹deservedly˺ honoured me!”

**The Third Movement Opens**

The sūrah's third movement opens in this verse, and the third movement is the movement of the vacillation. The sūrah's second movement stated the three peoples in their transgression and their punishment, and the sūrah now states the human tendency that follows the statement of the peoples, and the tendency is the tendency of the vacillation in the face of the fortune and the trial. The sūrah's third movement runs in the three verses, and the three verses are the verses of the boasting and the protesting and the vigilance that was stated in the closing of the second movement. The sūrah's verse is the sūrah's way of opening the third movement, and the opening is the opening in the form of the testing.

**The Standing Form of the Vacillation**

The Book states the vacillation in its standing verses, and the standing form is the form of the statement that the human being is the human being of the vacillation. "And there are some who worship Allah on the verge ˹of faith˺: if they are blessed with something good, they are content with it; but if they are afflicted with a trial, they relapse ˹into disbelief˺, losing this world and the Hereafter. The sūrah's five movements are the movement of the oaths in the five verses, the movement of the three peoples in the nine verses, the movement of the vacillation in the two verses, the movement of the rebuke in the four verses, and the movement of the Day and the address in the ten verses. The sūrah's structure is the structure of the five movements, and the five movements are the sūrah's complete form. The sūrah that opened on the oath of the dawn closes on the entry to the Garden of the Lord, and the closing is the sūrah's way of placing its argument in the two ends of the Event. The sūrah's last word is the word of the Garden, and the Garden is the Garden that the sūrah's first oath promised in its dawn.
